title: I can't code. I'm building a persistent multiplayer racing team manager with Claude Code, and here is what actually made it work
author: k2h1982
selftext:
I'm not a developer. I work in tech sales and I didn't touch any code for my school years, that's about it. Over the past few weeks I built Chicane Manager, a free browser game where you run a racing team in a persistent online championship: car design, drivers, money, and live strategy calls during a 3D race. It's about 20,000 lines of TypeScript (React, Three.js, a Node server), written entirely with Claude Code across roughly 200 commits. I never wrote a line myself.

I want to share what made the difference, because most of it had nothing to do with prompting.

**The first thing was treating it like a colleague with a bad memory**. I keep a short file of standing rules that gets loaded every session: never pause a live race, every visible text must exist in French and English, never deploy to production without my explicit go. Each rule came from a mistake that happened once. The file is the reason it didn't happen twice.

**The second was asking for scripts instead of trusting answers**. I can't review code, so I asked for tools that review the game for me. One script simulates full seasons and tells me if the economy drifts or if the AI teams become unbeatable. Another fails if any text is missing its translation. Before I see any UI change, it drives a real browser, takes a screenshot and looks at it. When it tells me "verified", I ask what exactly was verified and what wasn't. That one question caught more bugs than anything else.

**The third was two servers**. A sandbox where anything goes, and the real game, where real players have a season running. Every change lands on the sandbox first, I play it, then I say yes. It sounds obvious to developers. For a non-coder it was the single thing that let me ship daily without breaking a championship in progress.

**What didn't work: letting it design the game.** Left alone, it produces something reasonable and flat. Every decision that makes the game mine came from me playing and complaining. Two races a week because one felt too slow. A checklist for new players because my first testers were lost. A no-account trial because someone on Reddit told me a login wall was a hard sell, and he was right.

It's an alpha with a first full championship of 11 human players and a second one filling up. You can try it solo without an account at [https://chicanemanager.com](https://chicanemanager.com). To join the online championship, sign up with the invitation code **reddit-aigamedev**.

Happy to answer anything about the workflow, especially from other non-coders. What do you use to check work you can't read? Or do you even check work or just focus on the outputs and the "taste" of the game ?

comments.author: ScrywareDev
comments.body: The rules file part is real. Mine started the same way, every rule in it is there because something went wrong once. Deploy does not happen without my say so, that one is in there in bold. Question for you: how do you keep it from growing forever? I keep adding and almost never take one out, and I am starting to wonder if the old ones stop earning their place.

replies.author: k2h1982
replies.body:
Honest answer: I don't prune it myself. I let Claude maintain it, the same way it maintains the code. What helps most: whenever a rule can be checked by a script, it becomes a script. "Every new text needs its English translation" is now a check that runs before deploy, so it left the rules file.

More broadly, I trust it with the technical side and keep my attention on the gameplay: what feels fun, what feels unfair, what players complain about. The one thing I never delegate is the same as yours: nothing goes to production without my say so.

Do you review your file by hand, or do you ask the model to audit it?

replies.author: ScrywareDev
replies.body: The script part is the bit I have not done in an organized way. Most of mine are still just text the agent has to remember to follow, and that only works until it does not. How do you decide which rules are worth turning into a check and which ones stay as judgment calls?

replies.author: k2h1982
replies.body:
Two questions decide it for me. Can a machine tell whether the rule was followed? And has it already been broken once? If both are yes, it becomes a script.

Examples from my project: "every visible text needs an English translation" is a script that fails the deploy if one is missing. "Check the game balance after any gameplay change" is a simulation that plays thousands of races and prints the win rates, so I can see if a change made the AI too easy or too hard.

What stays as a judgment call is anything about taste or risk: is this fun, is this fair to players, should this go to production now. Those stay with me. The agent gives me the numbers and I decide.

A good trigger: the second time I have to remind the agent of the same rule, I ask it to write the check itself.

replies.author: ScrywareDev
replies.body: The broken once part is the bit I had not put into words. Most of mine stayed as plain text until something broke, then I wished I had scripted it earlier. Do you script it right after the first break, or wait to see if it happens again?

replies.author: k2h1982
replies.body:
Honestly, I don't have a fixed policy. I'm not a developer, so I rarely think "this should be a script" myself. 

What happens in practice: I state the rule in plain words, for example "the game must be fully bilingual" or "check the balance after every gameplay change". Claude is usually the one that proposes a check and writes it. My part is saying yes and then asking for it to be run.

So the timing is mostly "as soon as the rule exists", because writing the script costs me nothing. Your question makes me think I should maybe ask for it more deliberately after a break.
